utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Mr. Court Deputy.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is Case Number IT-02-60-T, the Prosecutor versus Vidoje Blagojevic and Dragan Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, before we have the witness, are there any matters that the parties would like to bring to the attention of this Bench? Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. As you know, Mr. Karnavas and I have been talking about the -- just the upcoming schedule to try and get an idea of where we are so we can arrange the witnesses that are coming. As you know, we have one witness that is here from Bosnia that is -- will be ready to testify tomorrow or Friday, and I know there's different options that were possibilities, including going later or bringing witnesses later. But we -- just any helpful directions you had on that we will clearly take and arrange our witnesses accordingly. And I'm sure you know that Mr. Deronjic has a three-day sentencing scheduled next week, Tuesday, Wednesday, and Thursday. I don't see his lawyer this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, actually we did not expect that cross-examination for Mr. Deronjic will take that long. So, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm trying to speed it up as much as possible, but I must say, every night I go over the material. There's thousands of pages. Frankly, this is a three-week witness, but I'm not asking for that. The next witness that the Prosecution has is a one-day witness. We can -- I've looked at it, went over it with Mr. Stojanovic yesterday, that testimony. And we anticipate that based on direct and cross, that witness can be on and off the stand in one day. There's a limited -- there's some limited issues on that. With respect to Mr. Deronjic, we are now about to be engaging into areas that are much more -- that are relevant -- much more relevant to this case, but as you can see, the chronology is vital. And we're going to be going over his background and we're going to be going over -- and that is terribly necessary and this has been necessary because at some point we need to be discussing his alleged conversations with President Karadzic outside the presence of anyone else. I should also say that at some point I'm going to ask that we go into private session so that I can discuss the issue of Mr. Nikolic. And just as a heads up for the Court, because I don't want to appear as if I'm trying to be cavalier about what I will be asking Mr. Deronjic. I would like the opportunity to ask him whether he would be willing to repeat his testimony with respect to what Nikolic told him if Mr. Nikolic was here in court and that that could be arranged, for Mr. Nikolic to be here, so that we could have sort of in a civil law procedure a classic confrontation. I see that Your Honour -- you're shaking your head. But I certainly think that it goes to the credibility. And I certainly would like the opportunity to have Mr. Nikolic here and also cross-examine Mr. Nikolic about this. As you can see I'm trying to do the best I can to shed light in this manner. But in any event, I take it with the Courts -- with Mr. President's reaction, that I should not entertain, let alone ask the question, What if Mr. Nikolic would be here -- or could I ask that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course you could make any requests you believe that is proper, but on our part we have to look into the proceedings and the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, whether it's possible to accommodate your request. You haven't told me how long are you going to take for Mr. Deronjic. Is it possible for you to finish the cross-examination for Mr. Deronjic tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I would -- if we could go all day, all day, that is up to 4.30, I might be able to finish it, I might. This -- I must say that for the first time I feel somewhat constrained having these short days, because just about when I'm getting ready, you know, and we're getting our second wind into the matter, we end for the day. And -- because it takes a while to warm up the engine and get it to the point where we're moving at a faster clip. I think if I could have a full day tomorrow until 4.30, I could.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I could not give you an answer this moment, because I understand the courtroom arrangement is very tight. There are several cases going on. During the break I have to consult with the Registrar to see if there's any possibility for us to sit until 4.30 tomorrow afternoon, but we'll do our best. And on the other hand, I think that your cross-examination, which I must say is very good, but there's still a possibility for improvement. For instance, the discussions about language and issues we don't believe is necessary, whether Mr. Deronjic is an expert or not. And we also notice that as you know the list of the documents you are going to use is growing again this morning. So I just want to ask you, try your best to streamline your cross-examination, and meanwhile during the break I'll consult with the Registrar to see whether there's any possibility for us to find a courtroom to sit until 4.30 tomorrow afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I would have one request. I would appreciate if we don't make a formal announcement in front of Mr. Deronjic, because then he might get the impression that he can just go on with long-winded non-answers, as he is prone to do. I think the fact that he knows that he may be on for a significant period of time may be reasons for him to be somewhat more forth coming, and of course I will make every effort to be tighter, more streamlined, in my questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, of course we will not tell him about the time limits, but it is also our duty to warn him that he should answer the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: In very simple and concise language.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. Could we have the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Are you ready to start?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic, I think we are pretty satisfied with your testimony the last two days. But there's still some room for improvement. First of all, I believe that your answers could be very concise onward and up to the point. If there's more information that the Defence counsel will need, he will ask you the follow-up questions on that issue. Of course you have the right to explain some matters raised by the Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I agree. And I shall endeavour to be as concise and precise as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you. And the second matter is that as Mr. McCloskey raised before you came into the room that your counsel is not present in this courtroom. Shall we proceed without your counsel's presence in this courtroom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: So I guess that you give up, waive, your right to have your counsel here for today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do waive this right at this moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much for your cooperation. Mr. Karnavas, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During your direct examination, Mr. McCloskey asked you to explain why you might have been less than complete or less than truthful in answering questions to the Office of the Prosecution via -- to your indictment, and you indicated that one of the reasons was out of fear of where the interviews were taking place, at least the initial ones. Correct? That a fair characterisation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And yesterday you indicated that at some point - and I believe it was after you had become a suspect - you dismissed the lawyers that were being provided to you by the government of the RS and began to just meet with the Prosecution as a suspect in order to provide them with the information that they were seeking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as we discussed when I began questioning you, prior to your indictment you had approximately six meetings with the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is correct. I had maybe more than six meetings with them, perhaps seven. But I agree, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, the last meeting which took place on April 8th lasted for two days. So it was April 8th and April 9th, 2002. Perhaps that may account for the additional encounter.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, but there was one meeting which was not disclosed to the public. After that meeting we had another one which was held in the presence of the Prosecutor, Mr. Mark Harmon, which is perhaps what is causing confusion here. The topic of that meeting was to agree on cooperation if possible. That's what I had in mind. On that occasion no interview took place; it was just a meeting during which we discussed this possibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, that meeting to see whether there could be cooperation, was that before or after your indictment?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the indictment was issued. The indictment was issued two days prior to my arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where did that meeting take place, if I may ask?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was that with Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harmon was present, together with two investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Do you know whether that meeting was tape recorded?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was. All meetings must be recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I agree with you, they must, but not necessarily are. How long did that meeting take place, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it lasted one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We met in the morning pursuant to our agreement, and if I recall, I think we finished in the evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In -- after you were indicted and after your lawyers were provided with the disclosure material, were you provided with any material related to this meeting, the negotiating session, that you had that obviously was not disclosed to us in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to say that both parties undertook it not to disclose the meeting if necessary. This is what I requested, but you asked me a direct question and I'm bound to give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And my question is: Aside from the fact that it wasn't disclosed, that's an issue that we can resolve -- I can resolve with Mr. McCloskey, aside from that issue, were you provided as part of the preparation for your own case with any documents relating to that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We didn't ask for any documents. My lawyers are familiar with this. There was no giving of a statement, properly speaking. Facts were not discussed. I just explained to them the essence of what the issue was, and they know what it's all about.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did they tell you during that meeting or was there a discussion as to what they might be indicting you for, that is, Glogova and/or Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They didn't tell me at any point in time what I could be accused of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, what was the nature of the negotiations? I mean, they must have expressed some -- well, let me rephrase the question. Was this an attempt to get you to turn yourself in to the custody of the Prosecution or was this to see if you could come to some agreement as to what or for which event you should be indicted?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you an affirmative answer to any of your assertions, because there was no discussion about what I might be indicted for. Of course the Prosecutor made no mention at all -- although, I did ask a question at one point as to what I could be indicted for, but nobody answered, nobody discussed it. The objective of the meeting was to discuss whether I would agree on the assumption that I could be indicted, although at no point in time did they tell me that I would, whether I would agree to cooperate with the Prosecution. The term that they used was "substantive cooperation," whatever that meant, including giving testimony, and that there was a very great probability of my being indicted, but it was not directly said to me. All options remained open.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So this was a meeting to see whether you would become a cooperative witness for the Office of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We could say that this was the objective of the meeting, but I have to stress that I was in no way familiar with the meaning of the institution of a protected witness or with the term "substantial cooperation." The discussion turned around, what it actually was, what would be required of me, what would the Prosecutor expect from me, not mentioning the indictment which was apparent -- I mean, it was apparent at that point that I would be indicted. But it was not clear at that moment with respect of which events or incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And so at that period in time you were facing the possibility of being indicted, both for Glogova and for Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one told me either, but I was told, however, that the Office of the Prosecutor has enough evidence to issue an indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But in your own mind - and I'm trying to get to your state of mind - in your own mind you knew or you suspected that there was a great probability that you would be indicted both for Glogova and for Srebrenica, or at least one of the two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My feeling was, and it was based on a conversation with Jean Rene Ruez who was the one who questioned me most often and whom I knew was investigating the case of Srebrenica, I asked him whether he would summon me for another interview and whether it was possible for us to draw any conclusion as to my responsibility regarding the Srebrenica events and whether he, or rather, the Prosecution was intending to issue an indictment. And he said, I will quote his words to the extent I can remember, he said: Mr. Deronjic, at this point I do not think that you are guilty of the Srebrenica events; however, I am not in charge of issuing indictments. I have presented the results of my investigation to the Office of the Prosecutor and it is the Prosecutor who will adopt the final decision. However, if I may say, I don't think that you should be concerned too much on the basis of what I know. I, on the other hand, had a lot of things to worry about at the time, my family and so on and so forth, so I wanted to know as much as possible. And I also intended to surrender in case an indictment was issued against me. When I spoke about Glogova during this particular interview, a document was shown to me, a document originating from the military tribunal in Republika Srpska, to which tribunal I gave a statement in which I admitted my guilt with respect of the events in Glogova. And I knew at that point that any future indictment would be based on my participation in the events in Glogova.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At a minimum?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll deal with this issue at some other point. But now that we've covered that information, you indicated that after you dismissed your lawyers you began reading with the Office of the Prosecution, at their request and at their designated locations, which you had insisted to be outside of Pale or outside of government buildings because out of fear that there may be some leakage or some tapping of the information, the conversations, and you wished to speak freely to the Office of the Prosecution. And I'm paraphrasing, of course, but that's the gist of your testimony, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the testimony, in that he additionally said that he deliberately avoided -- he deliberately protected himself and Mr. Karadzic. And that is a misconstruction of the testimony, and I think it is improper.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't said anything about Mr. Karadzic. I don't know, maybe he's getting the wrong translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: No, no, no, Mr. Karnavas. I think your question is subject to various interpretations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll break it down, but it's rather far fetching, the one that I'm hearing from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At some point, Mr. Deronjic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, the gratuitous comments I would object to. I don't want to make a big thing out of it, but since time is of the essence, the issue that Mr. Karnavas keeps going over and over again is this one we've talked about where Mr. Deronjic has already admitted that he was not truthful with the Prosecutor and he's tried to protect himself, tried to protect Karadzic. And for various reasons, one including the reason Mr. Karnavas just said, that he was concerned about his security. Now, Mr. Karnavas has gone over and over this issue, and as is his right. But at some point it becomes so repetitive that it wastes time. And I think Mr. Deronjic has shown that he will continue to answer the questions the same way he did to me, the same way he did to Mr. Karnavas. And I don't know how many times he has to say that. It seems that we're getting repetitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may briefly respond. If the Office of the Prosecution does not wish for lawyers like myself to be repetitive, I suggest when they question witnesses and when they have qualified lawyers such as Harmon or McCloskey at those meetings, they should not be going over the same material over and over and over and over again. Why are they being repetitive. So I'm only working with their information. So if Mr. McCloskey thought it was necessary for their office to go over the same ground of material year after year after year, meeting after meeting after meeting, Mr. McCloskey has no basis and no right to stand here and suggest that I should not go into each and every statement. I'm entitled to this. And I think I've been rather quick to the point and I'm about to go into this area one last time and then we're going to leave it because there's one last statement. And I'm trying to make sure that I understand the witness and that the witness is clear as to why he was meeting the Prosecutor on April 8th and 9th in Banja Luka, the very last time he met with them before he was arrested, the very last time he gave a statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, I think your question is proper, but the matter we raised, it seems to me that there is no dispute about that. Both parties as well as the witness agreed that Mr. Deronjic made some untruthful statement previously, previously. I think that's why the Prosecution asked the witness many times before. So I hope you could conduct your cross-examination in an expeditious way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, you met with the Office of the Prosecution on April 8th and 9th of 2002, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That was in Banja Luka in and safe and secure environment that was provided to you by the Office of the Prosecution, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And by this point in time you had been talking to the Office of the Prosecution since February 4, or even before that --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, beginning with December 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... And so here we are four and a half years later or four years later, you do the math, and you are meeting with them yet once again, but this time in a place where you feel comfortable that you can speak freely to the Prosecution. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as safety is concerned, I did feel safe, certainly. If you meant fear that information may leak, I did get actual confirmation that information did leak, even from that venue. I was even informed that my statements reached the General Staff of the Army of Yugoslavia and that they were reviewed by Mr. Vujin and studied by the General Staff. So not that I had misgivings, I had absolute certainly that my statements did leak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So they must have been leaking from the Office of the Prosecutor because at least the other statements that you were being given, at least the one in 12 March 2001 was also given - I'm not finished with the question, Your Honour - was given in Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, that's an allegation. There should be some --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not suggesting that they were leaking but he's made the point, Your Honour. He's made the point, so there can only be one other place. Now he's no longer in a government building, he's with the Office of the Prosecution. And I certainly am not alleging that they're leaking information, but the gentleman seems to be making that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: The question that you put, you may say that, are you suggesting that --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I could phrase it that way, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could go into closed session very briefly, I might be able to help this situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, prior to your meeting of April 8th and April 9th of 2002, you had been gathering as much information as you good about the events in Srebrenica or about what the Office of the Prosecution might have as far as documents that could possibly tie you in to the events of Srebrenica. Is that not a fact, Mr. Deronjic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I regularly did that to the extent of my possibilities, to the extent of my ability, in order to prepare as best I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Because after you had been declared a suspect and after Mr. Ruez refused your request to tell you exactly what portions of the your statement had been responsible or were responsible for the changing of your status from witness to suspect, you began trying to find information in order to have answers for the Prosecution in the event or during the events of your questioning?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already answered this question. I always try to gather as much information as I could.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I know. But see, my question -- that question was designed to motive, motive in order to -- you know, one is, yes, this is what I did. The next question was: Why did you do it? And of course if I were to ask you why, I suspect the answer would be because you wanted to have information so you would have time with you and perhaps your friendly contacts to form chronologies or to form coordinated answers in the event you or others were being questioned by the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as some events are concerned, I tried to put things together as far as I could. And I had my own reasons. I don't want to repeat them. And I adhered to that position until the bringing of the indictment. And to this day I don't want to say that this was the only reason for my decision, there were several reasons, but the fact is that is what I decided and I am abiding by it. Certain sensitive things that I judged could harm President Karadzic and could perhaps harm my personal status, I decided to keep quiet about. The confusion, if you allow me Mr. Karnavas, the confusion about that second meeting, when I mean that there are things I decided to leave out, they have to do mainly with that second meeting in Pale and my conversation with Mr. Beara, which I could elucidate if you ask me specific questions. But with regard to my second visit to Pale, the confusion was created when I received information from my friends that we had entered Srebrenica on the 14th of July. I will name names: Mr. Petko Pavlovic, chief of the security station in Srebrenica; Bane Katanic [phoen], who later became president of the municipality in Srebrenica; and some other people who all claimed in unison that we were in Srebrenica on the 14th of July and that we set up civilian authorities there. The truth is that they all did enter, but that didn't include me. And the fact that they entered Srebrenica on the 14th of July was something with which I couldn't fit in, my own visit to Pale. And that's the reason why I left that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, we're going to be here for the next couple of weeks if you continue to answer questions in that fashion. All right. Now, that was not the question that I asked. Let me be concrete about it. Were you not in Belgrade, according to your previous statement, a statement that you gave on 12 March 2001, where you assert, and I'm quoting from page 13, you assert that you accidentally -- you said: "I accidentally got a text where it was stated that this was recorded, the conversation between President Karadzic." And you're referring to your conversation with President Karadzic on the night of the 13th, that intercept. Okay. Now, my question is: Based on your assertions here, is it not a fact that you were in or you claim to have been in offices in Belgrade that were devoted to the investigation of crimes in Bosnia where you were searching for documents trying to find a way to learn as much as the Prosecutor had on you so you could concoct and create and manufacture and fabricate answers that would somehow get them to believe that you were not involved in Srebrenica in any way, shape, or fashion?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reply is yes. But in your question you made an assertion that I went to Belgrade in order to get some documents. That is not accurate. I had already told the Prosecution that in Belgrade on one occasion I received an invitation from a person who asked me to refute a piece of news that had been published, and he brought a transcript, in fact a recording of a conversation between me and Karadzic, and asked me to refute it, to deny that it happened. I refused to do that and I had no opportunity to even investigate further in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, by 2002, when you are being questioned, by this point in time, you know for a fact that the Prosecutor is keenly aware of your participation in the events in Srebrenica and is particularly insistent in getting an accurate account of what happened during those critical days. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And on this particular two-day session that you had, April 8th and April 9th, 2002, Mr. Harmon, a Prosecutor whom I believe you have come to be -- to spend some -- quite a bit of time with, was asking questions as well as the investigators. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At that last official interview, Mr. Harmon was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, he was not merely present, he was also asking you questions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would take it that by the fact that a Prosecutor was asking questions, that might have, at least in your mind, made the questions somewhat more significant?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. In other words, you were going to be as truthful with Harmon as you had been with Mr. Ruez and all of the others?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The decisions that I had made earlier I did not change on that occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Were you trying to be honest and truthful with Mr. Harmon on that occasion, or were you trying to fabricate and provide false information; which of the two?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: How on earth can I be completely sincere and honest? I am repeating for the umpteenth time that I had decided already to leave certain things out. It is up to you to understand that as you wish. That's your right and I don't want to interfere with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, there's a difference between omitting to tell the truth and deliberately providing false information. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And so if I understand your answer correctly, on April 8th and April 9th, 2002, you were not providing false information, but rather, you were omitting some conduct of yours that might somehow get you involved in a Srebrenica indictment?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's compound, which makes it extremely difficult to answer. I have no objection to both questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Why don't we see if the witness can answer the question before Mr. McCloskey jumps up and down. I think the gentleman is quite averse to answering questions and he's quite clever and very, very intelligent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: You know the objections should be before the answer, otherwise it's meaningless. Secondly, as for this question, I don't think it's a compound question. Mr. Deronjic, do you understand that question? Can you answer it? If you have something that you are not quite clear, you could ask a question to Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I understood the question, Your Honour. I will answer. Here it is: I agree with your assertion that I tried to provide accurate information about those things that I thought did not risk to establish a link between me and Mr. Karadzic. I tried, as I say, but I'm not saying that I have indeed told the whole truth at that moment and perhaps it is also true that I didn't even know the whole truth at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So it's not that you were trying to protect Mr. Karadzic, because after all he had been indicted; you were trying to protect yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: And Mr. Karadzic, I have already said that. Because the roles we played are in some ways linked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. We're going to talk about that. But before, if I could with the -- I could direct your attention now. I'm going to refer to this transcript, and it's page 131. This would be April 9th. I will provide you with the version.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: For the record it's going to be marked for identification as D98/1. And, Your Honours, we do not have the entire translated version of both days, because it was not provided to us. But the segment that I am about to confront Mr. Deronjic with or for which I want him to look at was translated. I would be asking the Office of the Prosecution to translate certain other portions or, at a minimum, we have the tapes readily available so Mr. Deronjic could listen to what he said. And we could talk about this during the break. I will talk to Mr. McCloskey about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I'm showing you a portion of your testimony -- or your transcript, your statement. This was given on April 9th, 2002. It's an official translation from the Office of the Prosecution. And if you could first look at page 6, line 10, and read it all the way through to page -- let's keep it simple, page 7, all the way through page 7. If you could do that. And for --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to be looking at, Your Honours, pages 131, 132, 133, 134, 135 in this segment of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If you could just look at that very quickly, Mr. Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have read that part that I think is of interest to you. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Now, if -- on page 132, and in your segment it would be page 6 somewhere after line 22, towards the bottom, you say that -- well, let's look at the whole point, the whole paragraph. It's titled -- on the side it's number 28.4. You state: "That was the order appointing me, the civilian commissioner for the region of Srebrenica. That is what is literally written. To be more accurate, that was the decision by the presidency of the Republika Srpska. And you know that that was a tripartite presidency. Mr. Karadzic, Ms. Plavsic and Mr. Koljevic. I heard about that decision at the time when I was with the soldiers in the trenches, in the trenches. As the president of the party, I thought it would be good if I was with the soldiers on the front line. And I received that" -- I'm sorry -- "and I received that through a radio or telephone link on the 11th. That decision was previously publicised in the media. When I say "previously," I mean on that day. Two policemen came to pick me up in Bratunac saying that Karadzic insisted on meeting me [unintelligible] Talking to me on the phone --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To talk with him urgently on the phone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: "To talk with him urgently on the phone. Thank you. I think I called him by telephone from the command of the brigade and I think -- as far as I remember now, the president told me on that occasion that that decision was made and that he was going to fax it to me. I don't remember whether that fax came to the SDS office or to the command, but I received during the night. I am talking about the 11th. I said as soon as I had read it I would go to Pale, and that was my physical contact with President Karadzic in those days." Now, let's stick with this at this point. From reading this text after you've had several years now to reflect and to come up with an accurate chronology, are you not suggesting here it was on the 11th that you physically received a faxed copy of the decision that made you civilian commissioner?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And that would totally contradict what you stated yesterday and the day before, that you did not get it until several days later, three or four days later I believe was your testimony, and that's why you were perhaps not fully aware of your full mandate as it related to the protection of the civilians, pursuant to paragraphs 4 and paragraphs 5 of that document?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour that's a very nice but there's no question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, he was answering the question before Mr. McCloskey interrupted. And I would appreciate if the Prosecutor would try -- would stop trying to obstruct. The gentleman listened, he has to wait for the interpretation as he reminded me and he has to answer the question. The gentleman can certainly say yes or no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But on the other hand, try to make your question as simple as possible. Your question constitutes about five or six lines in the transcript. I understand that your --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well. Fine, Your Honour. I'll switch styles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, as stated before, a statement such as this -- and I don't disagree with anything Mr. Karnavas is doing subsequently. But the Rules of adversary procedure require him to use this as either something to refresh his recollection or something to impeach him. If he had asked Mr. Deronjic: Were you in the trenches with the troops and Mr. Deronjic had said no, then he can impeach him with this. And I think that -- it would have taken a tenth of the time. That's -- reading a whole paragraph and then offering his opinions about it and asking Mr. Deronjic to comment on his opinions, the same point can be gotten to much more quickly and appropriately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, essentially I understand Mr. Karnavas's question. We see some contradictory statements yesterday and as well as on this document. So the question is to give the witness an opportunity to us why there is a contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Precisely, Your Honour. And if I were in the United States, I would be doing my cross-examination totally differently, but we're not. We're in an International Tribunal. I'm new at this game. Mr. McCloskey has been around a lot longer. I would suspect he would know that we don't apply American rules. But anyway.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let the witness answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Would you please answer that question.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand your question -- I'm sorry, I'm being interrupted by the interpretation. Yes, I understand your question. It is true that it follows from what I have been saying and what I said here in the interview, that there is a contradiction. You're right about that. With your permission, I would like to explain. I mean, you didn't ask a question about that but I expect that you want me to explain the contradiction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, before you explain the contradiction, let me inject a question and then please feel free to explain all you want. You would agree, would you not that based on your answer here, that one could draw the conclusion that in fact you were fully aware of your mandate on the night of the 11th, because you had physical -- you had physical possession of the document; and moreover, you had physically gone to Pale and you had spoken with President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't possibly agree with your assertion, Mr. Karnavas. It's interesting that first you say that what we establish is full of mistakes but if, however, correct. And then you're referring to something else that is erroneous and saying that it is accurate. It is your right to do that, but let me explain where this contradiction comes from. It is understood that what I said and what I have been saying, and -- or rather, compared with what I said in my last interview is correct and what I said in my previous interviews is not. And let me explain why. Now, I did not have this decision with me. It was not in my physical possession for a very long time. When I met with the Prosecutor, I found it, and for the reasons we've discussed -- we've been discussing over the last several days, because part of that documentation from the SDS was removed. You know that for a while I had an office in Srebrenica and that the institution of civilian commissioner and the president of the War Presidency functioned for a while. So we had a portion of the documentation there as well. You know that the Bosniak party won the elections, I don't know which year it was, and the documentation was removed as a result of that and so on and so forth. So I did not have the opportunity of finding -- of getting my hands on those decisions. When I saw it again, I realised -- I found out when it was adopted. And as for the conversation with Mr. Karadzic on the 11th of July, that is not in issue, I kept asking him to send me a document, the relevant document, with an explanation if possible. And we were discussing my -- the possibility of my visiting him at Pale. So this is what I was trying to remember. And at one point I thought that perhaps I did go to Pale that evening. I mean, I keep repeating this encounter. I was sure that during those days I went to Pale. However, when I found the document I believe that pursuant to the agreement that the president and I had, because he said, I would send you tonight or fax you tomorrow this decision, because I wanted the president to send me this decision so I was able to tell anyone, including General Mladic, that I had been formally appointed. When I came here and when it was decided -- when I decided that I should tell the whole truth without concealing anything and testify to the best of my knowledge, we still had to do some investigative work. I'm sorry that my lawyer is not here because he would be able to confirm that. I was able to remember a number of things, including how it was that I went to Pale, when exactly this could have been. And the way I remember it is because on the 14th I left with the Srebrenica people concerning an issue that they brought up on the 11th of the evening, and they protested --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness be asked to slow down, please. We're not getting everything.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may explain please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Slow down.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: So my intention was first to remember the reasons of my visit. And then it would be perhaps possible to me to remember when I went. So I was with the Srebrenica people, and I contacted the person by the name of Dane Katanic. Later he became the president of the municipality of Srebrenica. And he confirmed that he had been with me at the meeting at Pale on the 14th. So we were able to establish the right date of my visit to Pale and my encounter with Karadzic. I asked him about the details of the meeting, but I also asked him whether I had travelled alone or together with the delegation. And he said, No, you did not travel with us. So that's how things started to tally. And I remember certain things concerning this meeting. At this meeting at Pale, the president handed me this document, a copy of this document on my appointment. And it was on the basis of that that I was able to reach the right conclusion as to how it all happened. During the previous period of time for various reasons, people were not willing to cooperate, nor was it possible for me to go and see the president to ask him, Please, can you tell me when it was that you sent me this decision, if this is really relevant and important for you. Maybe it is. I have nothing against your believing this other version. I'm not taking issue with that. But once again, the president and I discussed the contents of the decision at that time. So I was familiar with my competences, although I had not received the decision on time. I insisted on an additional document, whereby my precise competencies and responsibilities would be defined, but such a document I never received.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, had you received that document, hypothetically speaking -- in other words, if what you're saying on the 9th is true and not a lie, that would be one more physical, concrete piece of evidence that would tie you closer into Srebrenica. Is it not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never disputed the fact that I was appointed with this decision. But I'm not a lawyer. I can make mistakes. The issue doesn't seem relevant to me. I always maintained that I was appointed on the 11th. I was given the decision subsequently. It contained my tasks. But the majority of that was cleared up in my conversation with the president. Formally, whether it was on the 11th or the 14th, as far as I'm concerned, I'm not a lawyer, is not important, is not relevant. But it may be relevant and important for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, when I have been pressing you on the point of the fact that you were in charge for the safety and well being of the civilians, have you not in this court under oath said, I didn't know the extent of my competency because I didn't have that document? Isn't that one of the arguments that you're raising here in this trial? Isn't that the fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But please, allow me to explain. You're talking about the decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The question was regarding the decision. Repeatedly you have said since you didn't have physical possession of that decision to read it, you didn't know your exact competencies, the exact orders that Karadzic had given you.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am saying this from my present position, in view of my present position. When I decided -- when I realised that I was given that decision directly by the president, unfortunately I cannot ask him, but it is from that position, in view of that circumstance, that I'm maintaining that I was given that decision on that time. Whether it arrived on the 11th or the 12th, that doesn't change anything. It does not contain enough information anyway. I wanted an accompanying document whereby it would be spelled out clearly what my responsibilities were, how I could use various instruments to implement the decisions that I adopt and so on and so forth. However, I never received a document to that effect. But it's a question that I should perhaps ask of the people who adopted that decision. It was not my intention to cause you problems concerning this issue, but I'm still maintaining that by and large I was familiar with the nature of my role. But that role was not explained in any better terms than it had been directly by President Karadzic over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So everything that you state in this statement with respect to going over -- going to Pale on the night of the 11th and speaking to Karadzic, who was in the presence of Mr. Krajisnik, who then -- he had left and you had a private tete-a-tete with the president, and everything that you discussed about General Mladic, all of this never occurred, as you have described it to Mr. Harmon?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're talking about the 9th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No. I'm talking about -- according to your statement here, if we go on to page 7, line 15, you say: "I found President Karadzic in front of the presidency. He was accompanied by Mr. Krajisnik." Now we're trying to implicate somebody else in the. "But soon he left. Mr. Krajisnik did not ask me anything. I talked to the president about the essence of the decision that he had forwarded to me. I told him that the decision was very difficult for me and did not provide me with the means to carry out." Now, it's time for the break. I think it might be useful if you could use -- read all the way to page 9, because I will put to you when we come back the question: Do we not get the essence from these pages that what you're trying to suggest is that you had a piece of paper but no power to carry it out, and therefore you could not be held responsible for the fate of all those citizens of Srebrenica that you were mandated to protect? That's the question I will be putting to you after you have a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, though you have already put it to me. You said we're going to have a break now?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to have a break -- I'm not controlling the court, but it's breaktime and I think the President would like to have a break. But I would like you to read those pages carefully because I will be putting forward the proposition that you were trying, in the best way you could, to show that you had absolutely no de facto or de jure powers to protect the citizens, in spite of that piece of paper. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we'll have our break. We'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, during the break did you have an opportunity to read the passages that I asked you to read or I suggested that you read?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And the passage that I pointed out to you, which is from what has been marked as D98/1 for identification purposes, it was an interview you had and this is from the 9th of April, 2002. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was it from April -- 8 April -- or 9 April 2002, or you're not sure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. And during that time you were being questioned by Mark Harmon, were you not, or someone by the initials of MH?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in the portions I showed to you, does it not conflict with your earlier testimony that you did not go to Pale on that evening, that is the evening of the 11th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What earlier testimony are you referring to? I mean, generally speaking, I'm not sure about the dates in all statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. In this particular statement, do you not state that you went to Pale on the 11th and that you met President Karadzic in front of the presidency with Mr. Krajisnik? Does it not state that? And this can be found in the English version on page 133.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And then it states, does it not, that you had a private conversation with Mr. Karadzic, that is, it was just a one-on-one with no one else present there to listen in to that conversation?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during this conversation you state to Mr. Harmon that you had expressed to President Karadzic your reservations with respect to being able to carry out the mandate, as it had been given to you and as you had reviewed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And earlier, as you spoke before the break, you admit, at least in this document, that -- and during this statement, that you had received the document, physically you had received it, via fax either through the office of the SDS or from the command post of the Bratunac Brigade, which is where you made contact with President Karadzic via phone.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This is what I say in this document. The answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, one of the reasons you state for going to Pale on that particular day immediately upon receiving the text is because you wanted to have clear guidance on how you would implement your functions as the commissioner of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not noticed this particular allegation, but I accept it, that this is what I stated as being the reason for that. But I cannot at this point find the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you wanted clarification of -- let me rephrase it. In the passages that you read, you appear to be telling Mr. Harmon that, one, you had a rather difficult relationship with General Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you were somewhat apprehensive as to whether you would be able to carry out your mandate, given that the document that designated you commissioner of Srebrenica did not give you authority over the military. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I was concerned about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at some point Mr. Karadzic assured you that -- or first urged you to just go and try to arrange some understanding with General Mladic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And he even indicated that he would be sending an order to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I assume, since this was -- assuming that this indeed took place, that is, the meeting in Pale on the 11th and your concerns and President Karadzic's assurances to you that he would be sending an order, assuming that that is correct, would it not follow logically that given your new position and your status as president of the SDS, that President Karadzic would have copied you with that order if an order was sent to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is logical. It's a logical assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I'm not assuming that everything that was done in those days or those years were done with any degree of logic. But logically if we were to follow Aristotelian logic, we could come to that conclusion could we not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, the answer is yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And at no time do you ever state anywhere that you had been copied with an order that might have been given by President Karadzic to General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I can assume then that no such order, written order at least, was ever provided to General Mladic, as far as your understanding is today?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wouldn't be my conclusion. I don't know anything about it. The fact that I didn't see it doesn't rule out the possibility that such an order does exist.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. But if we could just deconstruct that a little bit. Is it not a fair characterisation that President Karadzic and General Mladic did not get along very well during that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not have enough information to be able to confirm that. However, I do have some knowledge that the relations were not that good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you in fact -- and I don't have the passage here, but I will be -- I will find it and confront you with it. Is it not a fact that you have told the Office of the Prosecution in one of your interviews that there was friction and that often Karadzic would visibly and openly sort of get angry with General Mladic and his behaviour?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. However, I cannot conclude on that basis only what you suggested earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, after the fall of Srebrenica, General Mladic is kicked off his position, is he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware with the events after the fall of Srebrenica and the rift between the President Karadzic and him, yes -- to some extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well -- and the president did dismiss him, did he not, from his position of being, you know, the top general?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you can look at it that way, too. As far as I am aware of the order, it was to a point him coordinator between the Army of Republika Srpska and the Army of Srpska Krajina. I could not agree that he was replaced; he was replaced in a sense. But according to the order, he was appointed to a higher position, which as far as I am aware he refused. And all I know about it is from the press and from second-hand sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you are aware, are you not, that several generals signed a protest letter, one of them being also General Krstic, protesting the approval of General Mladic from his position? Are you aware of that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of the details. I did hear about it, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But at that period of time when there was in controversy with Mr. -- with General Mladic and President Karadzic, you were still a high-ranking member of the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that point I was a member of the main board, and I discharged those functions in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And being -- we're going to talk about your background just shortly. But being a member of the main board is rather a significant position, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is exactly what I said. The main board consists of 100 or so persons. It is up to you to judge how important the position is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were you happy to be promoted to the board after spending so many years as merely the president of Srebrenica -- president of the SDS of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was promoted to the main board, or rather, elected or loaned to the main board in the summer of 1993 after the party renewed its activity, after a one-year break. And since the member of the board from that area had been killed, Goran Zekic, that is, I was loaned to the board to replace him. I was not elected properly in summer 1993. Maybe, Mr. Karnavas, you meant my position as vice-president, to which I was elected in 1996, and I did spend one year in that position.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No, I didn't mean that. How many years were you on loan to the board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean how long I remained in that position? From 1993 to 2000 or 1999, when I resigned. I'm not sure. In any case, my written resignation exists somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And for that entire period of time, you were on loan, as you put it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In the meantime one party elections were held. And at those elections, my membership in the SDS was confirmed. And after I was replaced from all the other positions, I withdrew from the main board as well. But I have to add, and this fact can be verified, that in 1997 I did not attend main board sessions at all. You can ask why I didn't resign from that position as well. I was told that elections were coming soon and that it was impossible to loan somebody else, and that's why I stayed. But I didn't go to sessions anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, from this -- the passages that we have read -- that you have read, one would get the impression that what you are insinuating to Mr. Harmon was that you had this document, which was a piece of paper, but actually no power to carry out those functions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When you say "I insinuated," I suppose you mean that I was trying to make things look better for me. I don't see how really. Maybe there is some confusion, and if the Trial Chamber allows me, because this seems to be a key argument of yours, I would like to take five minutes to explain the matter and to remove any inclarity. If the Trial Chamber allows me, I would like to clarify this once and for all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I would like to go to the next question, Mr. Deronjic, as opposed to giving you the floor for five minutes, and then you can clarify it at some other point in time. You were complaining to Mr. -- President Karadzic that you did not have the necessary means to carry out his mandate, the mandate that he had given you. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. And that was the truth. I don't see how I can make you see if you won't allow me to explain. We were talking about this on the phone on the 11th in the evening --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I don't mean to interrupt, but we're going to go question, answer, question, answer --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, please. How can I tell you if you imply that I'm talking to Karadzic at Pale? I can't say yes to that. If you are implying some other possibility, then the answer would be, yes, we talked on the phone, and that's true. And if you want me simply to say yes, that would be untrue, because that would imply that we met. We've talked on the phone. If you don't allow me to remove this inclarity, I don't see how I can establish the fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I would object to any insinuations that Mr. Deronjic cannot explain his answers, though I would agree with Mr. Karnavas that perhaps five minutes is not appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe the word you used, Mr. Karnavas, is not correct, that is insinuated.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour. I understand. It was a conclusion perhaps that one wishes to draw on cross-examination, but I will rephrase.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From your -- just from the answer you just gave us, I take it the passages that you read during the break because you claim that this is a -- this is what happened in Pale with Karadzic, who you saw, with Krajisnik, and all the other matters that are related to these pages are false.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They are not true, yes. I have to make a distinction. It's not true that I was at Pale. What is true is that the conversation took place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. So when you told -- well, here you're trying to convey to Mark Harmon in the best way you can that you were telling President Karadzic that what he was asking you to do was virtually impossible. Isn't that the conclusion that you wanted him to draw?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is true. And I told President Karadzic that much, but not in a meeting but in a telephone conversation. And I can tell you more things about our comments regarding Mladic that we exchanged during that conversation. We used --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I just asked a simple question; you answered it. Thank you. Now, the next question is: Would it not be logical for us to assume that if you tell Mark Harmon that you were there physically in person talking to President Karadzic, looking into his eyes, having a tete-a-tete with him, that it would be more convincing that you were really trying to stress the point that you could not carry out his mandate than if you were trying to tell him, You know, I had this conversation, we had to speak in code, we had to worry about being intercepted, but here's all the detail. Doesn't it make more sense, if you were trying to be convincing, that at this point, close to five years after you had been initially -- had been approached, that you would want to convey to Mark Harmon, the Prosecutor, that you tried your best and that you merely had was a sheet of paper that in essence was meaningless, as far as you were concerned, because you could not carry out that impossible task that he had put on your shoulders. Isn't that logical?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, sir. And I really wish to assist. I agree that is logical, but logical is not always necessarily what happened. There are certain things that you seem to infer, and I cannot say that your inferences are illogical. However, there are other possibilities. I'm not saying -- I don't know exactly when this happened. I'm telling you about the substance of my statement, and never did I say "tete-a-tete, looking into his eyes," et cetera. I'm making no comments about that. In all statements I'm talking about the substance of our conversation. In my view, the substance matches much more than whether it was on the 11th or whether it was in direct contact or not. I agree, this is important and that it may cause some confusion. But it was a telephone conversation from the command of the Bratunac Brigade with an officer present. I don't know if there is a recording of that telephone conversation. I don't know whether the army taped such conversations at the time. I don't think this leaves much room for improvisation. If I can assist you further, I will tell you that I now remember the words concerning Mladic. He said, You know about number one, you know that my relationship with number one is disrupted. And there were many other details that I recalled later in the context of this conversation. But that I talked to Karadzic on the 11th on the phone at night is a fact; there are witnesses to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now let's -- happily, let's move on to another subject. In your statement of February 4, 1998, which has been marked for identification purposes as D93/1, you stated, and I'm quoting, this is on page 27 of the English version. But let me just give you -- it's a short quote. You say: "I was not in a position to receive an order from the president." Do you recall making such a statement to Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember; it's off-the-cuff. I have to find it. If you can tell me the page, if you are reading from somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I'll read you the whole segment. And on the English version, it's --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to read it out loud, just tell me which page it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just one second. I apologise for this inconvenience, but I'll read it while we're trying to search the place. You were asked by

utterances.speaker: MR. RUEZ
utterances.text: "Is there anything that you would like to add and we didn't raise during our conversation?" And at some point you say -- you will get it, just a second.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will read it and we will search for the page. You state, and this is on page 27, line 9 in the English version: "And I would like to point out that my relationship with the military structures, military authorities, was very complicated because they were dealing with issues of war and I was not in a position to receive an order from the president to give orders to the military authorities in relation to this evacuation of the population. Even if I was authorised to do something like that, I think that would have only aggravated that relation and made it more complex."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll take your word for it. There's no reason for me to read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm told that we don't have a translation of that part, but we do have the -- we could get the tape. Okay. So was it correct for you to state back then that you were not in a position to receive an order from the president? Was that a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That is a -- that's not a complete statement. It -- that takes it out of context. There's a few more words that provide it with the real meaning.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask the -- let me rephrase the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What did you mean when you said that you were not in a position to take an order from the president?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again, same objection --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In this context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Prosecution believes that there is some few words left out by you. Could you please add it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I don't know what he's talking about, Your Honour. I'll read it again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's simple. You're not -- what he says is he wasn't in a position to take orders from the president regarding ordering the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now that we have the Prosecution's version in cuing the witness. I think I can go on to my next question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's absolutely unfair for him to leave out the critical part of the thing. It's improper. It's unfair. I don't know if he meant to do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe if you want to read a statement, you have to read it concretely.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Let me read that portion again. "And I also want to point out my relations with the military structures, military authorities, was very complicated because they were dealing with issues of war and I was not in a position to receive an order from the president to give orders to the military authorities in relation to this evacuation of the population." Can you please tell us, what did you mean by that back on February 4, 1998?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I meant is this: I had not received any written authorisation, I called it order, that I was appointed to that function, to that position, and that I was entitled to give orders to Mladic and that he was under obligation to obey what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If we -- if I could go on to another matter before we -- I ask you questions about your background. In your statement given on 21 October 1999, which has been marked as D95/1 for identification purposes. At one point, and this can be found -- we have the translated version. For you it would be on page P33. I believe it's lines 12 to 20, but I'm only interested in one particular line. In the English version it's page 33, line 18. You state to a question posed by Mr. Ruez: "I am not such a big acquaintance of Karadzic, unfortunately." So I thought before we would go into your background, you could perhaps clarify to us, how is it that in 1999, October 21, you state to

utterances.speaker: MR. RUEZ
utterances.text: "I am not such a big acquaintance of Karadzic, unfortunately." How could you make that statement?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Will you give me the page number, please --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Page 33 --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- So that I can place it in context. My version is not paginated; I have to count.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. If I could have the assistance of -- Mr. Deronjic, I will help you out here. You were asked a question by Mr. Ruez a few lines earlier: "But the police who are supposed to be loyal to the president and inform the president if others are doing things which are not in the interests of the country might have spoken with you, since you are a close acquaintance with President Karadzic." Your answer: "I am not such a big acquaintance of Karadzic, unfortunately." And then you go on to say: "But I personally haven't talked about it, nor have I had any kind of information. To be straight as a human being, if it really happened, every information I'll get in possession, you know, I'll make available to you." Question: Was it true back in 1999 when you said that you were not a big acquaintance of President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I don't know what it says in the English version. And for the time being, I must note that you are not quoting accurately. What you have is a translation, and what I have is what I really said in my native tongue. Jean Rene Ruez is suggesting that I am a close acquaintance of Mr. Karadzic, and I told him: You know what, I am really not a person who knows Karadzic that well. How can you claim that I am a close acquaintance of Karadzic, whom I hadn't even known until the SDS was established? There are so many people who know him much better than I do. I never went to his house; I never socialised with him. It was constantly suggested in interviews and in other contexts that I was a very good friend of Mr. Karadzic, and that is absolutely incorrect. We had a strictly official relationship. I did know him, and we did get to know each other a little better when I became president of the party. And I said, place the emphasis properly, please, I don't know Karadzic all that well. If I had been such a good friend of his, he would have appointed me prime minister or something. You can judge by the function that he did appoint me to how well I knew him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let me just deal with it one by one. Does it not state, even in your version, that you are trying to suggest that you're not a big acquaintance of President Karadzic? Read exactly what it says, read exactly what your answer is --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. He's already done that and it sounded very similar. It's a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm entitled to do my cross-examination. And as far as wasting time, I'm entitled to pin this witness down because he's indicated and the Prosecution is going to argue that the reason why he was untruthful before was because he was trying to protect Karadzic and now we hear he hardly knows the man. This was 1995 he was being asked of Mr. -- President Karadzic. He just stated that even at that point in time he was hardly acquainted with the man. What we have here is the highest authority in Bratunac, a man who was solely responsible. The Prosecution has gone in front of the cameras and said, We don't have evidence to indict this man. They may have a reason why they wish to protect this gentleman. But I'm entitled to get to the truth and I am entitled to suggest that one of the reasons why he begins to fabricate after he's given his deal. That's what I'm getting at, Your Honour. And that's what I'm trying to -- I'll pin him down. Does he know the man or does he not. And if not, we're going to go through his background next. That's why I wanted him to give me an answer.
