Because When we go through his background it becomes crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe the witness has already read that part of his statement already and you have already asked this question before, at least once. So I think the question will be very simple: Does he know this man or not, as you said. It's a very simple question. Why make things more complicated for us?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas, I have to warn you about one thing. You have just said -- please, I haven't even answered the previous question --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I haven't asked a question, Your Honour. I haven't asked a question. I haven't -- there's no question posed to the witness. Mr. McCloskey objected; I responded; there was a ruling. I have -- there's no question posed to the gentleman.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's here Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas has had a long response which made some comments characterising certain things Mr. Deronjic had said. This is not generally appropriate for a response to an objection, and I believe Mr. Deronjic appears to be wanting to respond to what he said. And I don't see, given the comments, that that shouldn't be allowed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Let's hear what the witness is going to tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Karnavas is using every opportunity to make assertions. He says, for instance, a moment ago he said: Mr. Deronjic, in his statement, says that he hardly knew Karadzic. Let me read the sentence once again. I'm not going to say that it's just an insinuation. Let's say it's an omission. In this sentence I say: "You know what, and you realise how people get nervous when they say, you know what." So what I say is: "I'm not such a big acquaintance of Karadzic," and so on and so forth. And you are trying to say that I hardly knew Karadzic. Could you please identify those words for me? I cannot allow such qualifications, qualifications which have nothing to do with what I actually said in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Deronjic, I want to be very fair from you. I was reading from the text. The text here says that you know note to the question, Mr. Ruez, who is a trained investigator and whom we had the opportunity to meet here in court. He poses a question. He insinuates perhaps in his question, where he says: "You are a close acquaintance with President Karadzic." The question is why did you control the police and why are the police not responding to you since you were a close -- a big -- acquaintance. And your response, and I quote, is: "I am not such a big acquaintance of Karadzic, unfortunately." That's what it states in English. Does it state that in Srpski?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It says as follows: "You know what, I really don't know Karadzic all that well."

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you very clarifying that. Now -- and I apologise, because I'm reading the English version. I'm not trying to trick you. Could you please explain to us what you meant when you said you do not know him that well, given that the -- right now we're talking about 1999. You're being asked about events in 1995. And as we will learn when we go into your background, you had been closely associated with the SDS, almost from its inception several years earlier.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will answer your question, but please, Mr. Karnavas, you keep asking questions and then you proceed with qualifications of that question. So I don't know what I have to give an answer for. But let me try. With respect to numerous statements concerning myself that I had an opportunity of seeing, in a number of articles published during the war and after the war in the media, in particular in Bosnia, I was able to read all kinds of descriptions of myself. There was one that occurred often, which I remember very well. Miroslav Deronjic is Karadzic's right hand. What does it really mean? Legally, of course it doesn't mean anything. What does a right hand mean? What does a right arm mean? Also I read descriptions to the effect that we were close friends. I know what the truth is. And when you come to that, I will tell you exactly how the relationship between Mr. Karadzic and myself evolved. Now I'm skipping this because we haven't yet touched the subject. Here I became very irritated, and you can see this from the beginning of my sentence when I say: Now let me tell you, I'm not -- I don't know Karadzic very well. So this is what I said, and not what you're trying to suggest that I said to Mr. Ruez, that I was a big friend of Mr. Karadzic. I never went to see him at his home, nor did he ever come to my house, but we did meet from time to time. And I hope I will have an opportunity to explain that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So are you suggesting that we should accept the answer that you gave, that you did not know Karadzic very well? Should we accept that as being a truthful and complete answer?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not what I said. I'm just trying to say that we should agree as to the extent to which I knew Karadzic. I will tell you precisely when we come to that. But I have never said that I did not know Karadzic enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm using your own words, Mr. Deronjic. You say: "I did not know him very well." My question is: Is that true? Is it a fact that you did not know him very well? Is it a fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, yes, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: It's been asked and answered several times. The answer I most remember was that he was business colleagues with him, that they didn't go over to each other's house. This is a very typical response for such a normal question. And this beating this one phrase into the ground is a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with Mr. McCloskey. Mr. Karnavas, you may move on. And you promised the witness to ask some background questions. Maybe after those questions we could get a good sense of how well this witness knew Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I was trying to get a solidification of that before we went on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But let's talk about your background. Now, Mr. Deronjic, as I understand it, you are from the Bratunac area. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was born in that municipality, and I spent most of my life there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it at some point after graduating from secondary school, you went on to university. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I am correct, that was in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Where you completed your studies and you earned a degree?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And what was that degree in, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My title is professor of Serbo-Croatian language, that was the official name of the language at the time. Changes have occurred in the meantime. So I'm a teacher of the Serbo-Croatian language. I also have a degree in the history of literature, A and B. It was a double major. And also history of the literature of the Yugoslav peoples. I'm trying to remember the exact name.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, do you have a Ph.D., a doctorate degree, or were you double majoring or triple majoring when you were going to university?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I attended graduate studies, though. And I completed some exams, but I never finished, I never obtained a degree in post-graduate studies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, I take it after you finish your university education in Sarajevo, you went back to Bratunac to take a position as a teacher. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. For a brief period of time, for about two years, I worked in Sarajevo. And I continued with my studies at the same time. After that, I served my -- I did my military service, whereupon I returned to Bratunac. I worked as a librarian in the grammar school in Srebrenica for a while.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And what year was that when you started working as a librarian?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I entered on duty in September 1979, but I then went into the army, that is, I did my military service, my compulsory military service, because I wanted to get it over with. After I finished my military service, which was in the autumn of 1980, I went back to teaching, to this school.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- well, were you teaching in 1980 or were you a librarian? Which is it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You see, officially I was employed as a librarian. At the time the institution was already called a secondary education centre, but because I was a teacher I was often hired to do some teaching, which I did gladly. I used to like to teach. I don't remember exactly how long I did that. I think I followed through a whole generation, but I cannot exactly recall how long, how many years, I spent teaching.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, did you hold any other jobs before you came involved in politics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we take into account the jobs that I had in Sarajevo, yes, but they were not, strictly speaking, linked with teaching. For a while I worked at the local Sarajevo radio, then I worked at Ilidza in the local grammar school there, and then after that I went back to Srebrenica, so that's all. Yes, I forgot one thing. Between 1983 and 1985, I was in France. And I taught children of Yugoslav seasonal workers in France.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- and after -- between 1985 and 1990, did you hold any other jobs, other than being a teacher?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you specify the year? I mean, I didn't get the years.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, when did you become involved in SDS politics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I don't know the exact date, but it was in August 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: 1990, okay. And that's when the SDS party was being formed, was it not, if I'm not mistaken?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The party was established on the 12th of July, 1990, and preparations were underway in Bratunac until mid-August. But I didn't take any part in these preparations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, we're going to get to that. But before -- between August 1990 and the time that you returned from France, 1985, did you hold any other jobs other than being a teacher and/or a librarian?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, in Bratunac, I understand, the SDS was formed in or around August 1990. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The exact date is the 2nd of September. That is the official date when the founding assembly met. Preparations, however, were underway from May and June. At the same time, preparations were taking place at the level of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And who was elected as the first president of the SDS in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Miroslav Deronjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yet, Miroslav Deronjic was not involved in the preparation for the establishment of the SDS party in Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I was elected president at the first meeting I attended.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And how is it, I guess -- and I would like a your full and -- explanation. How is it that a teacher/librarian, with a couple of years out in France teaching workers, how is it that somebody like you who is not even involved in the formation of the party rose to the position of president of the SDS at its inception?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I myself am not fully clear as to how it all happened. I toyed with the possibility of establishing another party, and I spoke of that with the Prosecutor. I sort of hesitated between the SDS and Serbian renewal movement. I paid a visit to the leadership of those parties in Serbia as well. However, these concepts were not -- could not live in this area. Then I accepted an invitation of a friend to attend a meeting in Ljubovija in a nearby town in Serbia, where a party was apparently being established. And I knew it was about the SDS, which had already been established. I was curious and went there for information. I had never been a member of the League of Communists and I paid a high price for that. So, at that moment I wanted to become politically involved, politically active. So I went to this meeting in Ljubovija. The agenda had also the item of the appointment -- election of the president, or rather the representative of this party. I did not know the majority of the people there, and -- but however, they asked me whether I would be willing to accept this role. I was somewhat surprised, but I said, Why not. I must admit that I was quite ambitious at the time. So they voted on this proposal. I had one opponent, but I think I got all of the votes. And I was elected president of the SDS, or rather, the president of the coordination committee, which was on the agenda. But soon we had our assembly, our founding assembly, and this appointment was accepted. And I became president of the local SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: May I ask who was the friend that suggested that you go to this party, this party meeting, or this meeting in Ljubovija?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mikan Katanic is his name. He is a fisherman as well. We know each other as fisherman, and it was from the Drina that we went to this meeting in his car.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And prior to that, as you indicated, you were not involved in the League of Communists. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as I understand it, military officers were viewed to have been associated with the communist party, correct, or the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is how I viewed them, not all of them, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not all of them, but -- and I don't want to interrupt the flow of your background, but since we're here, during the years, during those war years, that was one of the reasons why there was constant conflict between the military and the civilian government was because the SDS was primarily non- and anti-communist, whereas the military was viewed as part of that old system. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By and large, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- moving along. At that point in time when you were voted in as president of the SDS in Bratunac or for the Bratunac municipality, who was the president of the SDS of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can we assume that Mr. Karadzic would have learned of your selection or election to that particular position?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I was elected president of the party on the 2nd of September, yes. He could have learned of that at the time, because there is written notification of that. As to the election, pre-election activities and various initiatives that preceded it, no, I don't think so. Because this was all based on the initiative of other members of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And before we go on, you mentioned that you were quite ambitious during that period. Would it be correct to assume that given your rise in that party, given your involvement over the years, that ambition never ceased from the period that you were elected president to after the fall of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, it would not be correct to assume that. I lost my ambition very early on. I can explain. I think I even gave an interview in which I took it upon myself to leave -- abandon all political functions once the war is over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, I'm not talking about once the war is over. The war was over after the fall of Srebrenica. So my question was: Did your appetite for ambition to move up the ladder in SDS politics, did it cease during that period of time or did it remain constant, if not ever so increasing?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite the contrary. My ambition became extinct in 1992. The interview that I mentioned was given in 1992. The name of the local paper is Nasa Rijec. It is based in Bratunac. I was disappointed with the events that took place in 1992. And I said -- I took it upon myself to leave politics by the end of the war, which gives you a clear indication as to how ambitious, in terms of politics, I was in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll talk about that as we go down your background. But when you say -- when you refer to the events of 1992, are you referring to the events in Glogova in 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the events that took place in 1992, from April, perhaps even before April, up until late June when this period was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to talk about it right after the break. We'll move on next and we'll discuss the period of 1992 somewhat extensively. But isn't it a fact, Mr. Deronjic, that after the sacking and the burning of Glogova, you went to Pale where, in essence, after giving a report about what had occurred under your leadership, you were congratulated?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean I was congratulated? I had an applause when I said that, but please be precise as to the reasons why I went to Pale. I didn't go there to get an applause; I went there to tell what had happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. And I was trying to get you to come up with the appropriate language, which was that you got an applause from the audience that was there listening to you describe your victorious campaign in Glogova when it was sacked and burned under your leadership as the president of the SDS at a time when, you now state, you were losing your appetite for SDS politics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again you have made certain qualifications with which I cannot agree. You used the term "victorious campaign." That is certainly not correct. I went there to say what had happened. And it is true I was a local leader, a leader from Bratunac, and I thought that it was necessary for me to tell them what had happened. I didn't go in the spirit that you have described. I was very concerned. I went there to tell the people what had happened. And the minister -- the president of the government, that is, Mr. Djeric was very angry. I wanted all of the relevant structures to be familiar with what had happened and if I were responsible -- even if I were responsible. And this is what happened and this is what I wanted to say, to tell them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to continue with your background. And then at some point when we get to 1992, we'll extensively discuss Glogova and you'll be given every opportunity to discuss your full involvement in those events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Mr. Deronjic, I believe we left off where you had just been appointed president of the SDS for Bratunac municipality. If you could please give us a description as best as you can as to the powers that are accorded to or were accorded to the president of the SDS party in a municipality at that time.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot give you a precise answer to this question because that is regulated by the statute, and that is a well-known document. I don't want to improvise on this. I had the regular authorisations, as envisaged by the statute of the party.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How many other parties, political parties, were involved or were in existence and operating during that period of time in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Bratunac, in addition to the SDS, if memory serves me well, there was an SDP, the restructured League of Communists; then the movement for Yugoslavia, the full name was the League of Communists' Movement for Yugoslavia; then the SDA, the radical party; and I can't remember any others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And do all -- did all these parties have the same power, either it be de jure or de facto, in the Bratunac municipality during the period, say, of 1992 to 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. At the 1990 elections, the SDA got the majority of seats, followed by SDS, and the third ranking was SDP, they won 5 per cent. We could say that the rest of the votes in proportion to the composition of the population reflected the ethnic composition, because Bratunac was populated mostly by Serbs and Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. I had asked a question with respect to 1992 to 1995, not 1990. But be that as it may, in 1995 how many of these parties exercised power in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two parties: SDP remained in the parliament, representatives of the Serbs, that is; and SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you did not hold, as I understand it, any executive positions throughout the entire period while you were president of the SDS and I say executive positions in Bratunac, in Bratunac municipality. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Save for my position as president of the Crisis Staff, which was de jure and de facto executive position. In the remaining period, I did not have any executive authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And not having any executive authority did not mean that you did not have power. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Depends on what you imply, de jure or de facto. De jure, I had no authority; as far as de facto is concerned, it is a matter for debate and that is a complex issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Is it fair to say that de facto you had quite a bit of power in Bratunac during those years. Is that not a fact?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the extent that that is accurate. Do you want me to elaborate?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not yet. We're going to get to that. Now at what point did you become president of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the end of April 1992. Just one more thing. There were two Crisis Staffs, one within the SDS was set up in November or December 1992, I have records here so we can verify, whereas the municipal Crisis Staff, I was appointed president of that staff in April 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And that's the one you were president of, the municipal Crisis Staff. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you said that there was a Crisis Staff within the SDS that was set up in November. Were you the president of that Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So both times you were president?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as president of the Crisis Staff, I would suspect you had quite a bit of -- you had lots of power, both de jure and de facto?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in addition to that, you were also president of the SDS. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at that time the order had already been taken to freeze the work of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But at some point you came back and the SDS was working quite energetically, was it not?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection as to vague. The various organs are so different between 1995 and 1992. If we could just get more clarity on date, I think that would make a better record.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. And the question you posed to this witness is too broad. What do you mean by quite energetic? It is subject to many interpretations. It is difficult for the witness to answer, so please be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour, very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Deronjic -- well, let's focus on the period when you were the president of the Crisis Staff. Was it during that period when the incident in Glogova occurred?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And prior to that incident, or perhaps even during that incident, there were also ongoing problems in Bratunac with relations to or as regards to certain volunteers who had come into the municipality. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And these volunteers, if I understand it correctly, their whole purpose, or at least their main purpose was to create terror in the minds of certain individuals in that municipality, primarily those of -- that were Muslim, in order to get them to voluntarily leave that area. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was their main purpose, to create an interethnic conflict and maybe make them leave, but not to make them leave by force.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. So it would appear, at least, that this was a voluntary action on their part?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On whose part?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That it was a voluntary action on the part of those leaving, the Muslims, that they were voluntarily leaving as opposed to being forcibly removed.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There's no question of that; nobody leaves their home voluntarily. People leave out of fear or because the conditions no longer allow them to stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when the volunteers came, you were the president of the party, correct, of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You were also the president of the Crisis Staff, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the SDS, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Of the SDS. And during that period, as I understand it, and I might be wrong, for the Bratunac municipality there was also a TO, a Territorial Defence, set up?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The TO had not yet been set up. It was set up when the Yugoslav People's Army arrived in Bratunac.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But that was sometime in April when it was set up, was it not, prior to Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, towards the end of April, the beginning of May, the staff of the TO was formed out of the people who had remained, mainly Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the volunteers were still around, were they not, or had they all left by that point?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. A group of them was still there. Some had been killed. They -- some came, others left.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now -- and one individual who I believe was a close associate, if not perhaps a friend of yours, was associated with the volunteers, was he not? And I believe you know who I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. Tell me who that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Goran Zekic, does that name ring a bell?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does ring a bell. He was a close associate of mine. I would even say he was a friend. And he was indeed connected with the arrival of volunteers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Not only was he connected, but he was partaking in some of the acts of terrorisation at the time, was he not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not that familiar with events in Srebrenica. It could be concluded from what I know that he had taken part, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, it was during one of those occasions that I believe he was ambushed by Naser Oric and his organisation or his colleagues, where Mr. Zekic was killed. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I wouldn't say Naser Oric, though. It was a group of Muslims. I don't have any information to the effect that it was Naser Oric precisely. But a group of Muslims ambushed them killing Goran Zekic. It happened the 8th of May. I even know the name of the man. He was even awarded the order of golden lily, posthumously.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And Goran Zekic and you were had been associated with and were working together in bringing arms into the Bratunac area, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On one occasion, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And when -- Goran Zekic was also, as I understand it - and I might be wrong - I believe he was also involved in the SDS party and a member of the board. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. At the outset, Goran Zekic was involved together with me in the attempt to establish some other party. And when the SDS was formed in Srebrenica, he was on the municipal board. After 1992, he was a deputy. And from the beginning, he was a member of the board of the SDS in Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And was it his death that allowed you the opportunity to move up the ladder or sort of make a lateral move to also become a member of the board?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. His death did result in my loaning to the board of the SDS, but only after 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Okay. And incidentally, if I could go back to something you said earlier. You said in 1992 your appetite for ambition or your ambition, I should say, for SDS politics was waning, was on the down side, you know. And yet, here we have 1993, you becoming a member of the board, filling in a slot of the late Goran Zekic, a close personal friend of yours with whom you were bringing arms into Srebrenica, who was also involved in acts of terror as you have described in your previous statements. Can you give us an account. How is it that you were losing your appetite, yet at the same time you were accepting positions?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope my answer will satisfy you. The war broke out in Bratunac, in Srebrenica, and in the broader territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. And of course when I received the offer to be loaned to the party, I had consultations, and everybody around me thought it would be very useful for Srebrenica and Bratunac, which became the hotbed of that war, if I can put it that way. I accepted the position and I accepted their arguments. Sometimes you accept a position for good, justifiable reasons, and that doesn't necessarily mean that you have the underlying ambition. Let me just add that no one from Bratunac or Srebrenica at the time held an important position on the regional or republican level. And if I had declined the position, I suppose that we would have been left without any contact with the top echelons in the republic in the conditions of war, and that would not have been a good idea, I thought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Now, in 1992, sometime in May, there was an attack on Glogova. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during that attack you, as the president of the SDS and president of the Crisis Staff, was involved, personally involved, in that attack, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, to the extent that I explained in the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Well, I guess let me be more concrete. You were at the scene at the time of the attack. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you mean the village of Glogova when you say the scene, that's not quite true. I was several kilometres away from Glogova fulfilling a specific task. That's what I explained in the factual basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, was it not you that ordered that a tank fire into a house and then torch it in order to create panic and fear? Was that not you acting in your capacity as president of the Crisis Staff and president of the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. That's what I said, in fact requested, at the meeting that took place just before that operation. Not in Glogova itself, I wasn't there issuing the order, but that's what I requested to be done at the meeting that preceded the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And I take it that the house that would eventually -- or that you were asking for to be fired upon was sort of indiscriminately picked. And what I'm trying to suggest is in doing so you were totally -- you were being totally indifferent as to whether there would be men, women, children, elderly in that house. Your point was to make a point to cause terror and perhaps even kill innocent people. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You drew the worst possible conclusion, and I agree it's possible to draw it. In all my statements, especially in the factual basis, I did not make a defence case for myself. I can give you the details, if you wish. I told them to shoot at the roof using, if possible, a lighter weapon. I didn't say they had necessarily to shoot at the house itself. I said they could shoot at an auxiliary structure. But it was not then in my mind that they should go out and kill somebody.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you didn't ask or you didn't order that they first try to identify an empty structure, so at least if they were going to make a point, they would make it in a way that there would be no loss of life. Because after all, as a family man, and you know the importance of a family, somebody might in there and might get killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. The witness has agreed with Mr. Karnavas's first very clear, descriptive description of this horrendous act. Now, any further goings into this is really not relevant to the case, and it's not appropriate. We -- the details of 1992 Glogova have been pled guilty by this man. And I am not objecting to the high points of these things, but the actual detail and the repetition of things that have already been brought out I don't think are necessary for this particular trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, in this point we tend to agree with the Prosecution. I think there is a factual base attached to the plea agreement or the facts that during that time was there. So there's no need to go into the very details of each instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I was merely trying to make the point that he had the power to order to fire at a house, just as well he had the power to order to fire at a structure that was not occupied, but he didn't do so. In other words, he had a total indifference to life. But I will move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, please move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please. May I just state one fact?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, the Defence counsel agreed to move on, so let's move.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, when you were questioned by the Prosecutor, Office of the Prosecution, back as late, I believe, as April 8 and 9, 2002, I believe that you were maintaining that at that time you were simply, and merely had the rank of a soldier during that incident. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And I could say the same today. I was an ordinary soldier in a unit which had its commanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And at that time the commander of the Territorial Defence was Momir Nikolic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So if we draw the logical conclusion, as we must, that you as president of the SDS and president of the Crisis Staff during this campaign against Glogova, you were merely subordinate, a mere foot soldier, serving within and under the ranks of Momir Nikolic, someone who was also, I believe, a member of the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Momir Nikolic was not a member of the Crisis Staff, unlike what you said. But by virtue of his position, he attended meetings of the Crisis Staff. Your first question, though, was whether I was a regular soldier. What has changed about my joining in, volunteering, if I was a member of a TO unit obeying the command of that unit, Mr. Mile Bozic was the commander of that unit, which I accompanied on that mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. The reason I mentioned that he was a member of the Crisis Staff incidentally was in your statement to the Prosecutor back on April 8th, and I'm referring to D98/1, when posed a question: "Momir Nikolic was a member of the Crisis Staff?" Answer, page 42, you say: "That is correct. That's the reason But in any event he was attending these meetings because he was he was the commander."

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. It's just a difference in interpretation. Some people were members by appointment and other people attended meetings by virtue of their position, ex officio, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: How is it that you as a member of the SDS and, a president of the SDS, and just a member of the Crisis Staff, how were you able to give a direct order to someone within the Territorial Defence who already had a commander, that is Momir Nikolic, how were you able to give a direct order for them to fire at a house? Were you exercising your de facto powers?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not issue an order to a member of the TO. It was a member of the JNA, Captain Reljic who is captain by rank. In fact, it was not the issuing of an order. I wrote a request for the army to take a firm position, and that's a demand I made from the army. As to the exercise of my powers, the fact that they did not fire a single bullet in Glogova speaks volumes. I tried to get them to provide some encouragement, but the fact is that they did not do as I asked and that JNA unit did not fire a single round.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, at some point there were atrocities as a result of this incident, correct, that is the attack on Glogova?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The relevance of --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're going to get there, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: There are so many atrocities in 1992, but we have our own share in 1995, which are clearly directly relevant. But 1992?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Your Honour, I will make it very plain and simple. It may be hurtful to the Prosecution, but it will be plain.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: During those atrocities in 1992 in Glogova, those are the ones that you have entered a plea of guilty. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I cannot agree with that. I pleaded guilty to the extent it was accepted by the Prosecution that I did not order, that I did not kill, that I was not present, that I did not know of those events, but that I was responsible, having ordered the action. And I think the phraseology used was that I should have forecast that this could happen. I cannot remember the exact words. I did accept that and I pleaded guilty to that; I confessed to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I agree. Now, if we are to use logic, would it not stand to reason that Momir Nikolic, who was the commander of the Territorial Defence and was also involved in this massacre, should have also been charged by the Office of the Prosecution for those deaths and those atrocities? Isn't that an extension of pure and simple logic?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas's well-known viewpoints of the Office of the Prosecutor are not relevant to his questioning of this witness. And he's assuming facts that have not been established. It's inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, we understand your point in asking this question, but we don't think that is a proper question to be posed to this particular witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Momir Nikolic at some point, after the VRS was established -- the Bratunac Brigade was established, became a -- the head of the intelligence and security sector of the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it's an established fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you knew that at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At what time? I cannot remember. It was not that important for me to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. But I'm saying during that period. From the moment that he was appointed all the way until after Srebrenica, you were aware of his status in the community and also within the Bratunac Brigade. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And in fact, in reading some of your statements, you seem to indicate that it was your opinion that he was in charge of the military police of the Bratunac Brigade. That would be as part of his function?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And as far as I know from reading your documents, there were times during those critical days in July of 1995 when you had requested or ordered the assistance of military police from the Bratunac Brigade, at least that's what I've been able to glean from these documents.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Just to be more precise, requested and suggested to them that they requested.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But at no time, at no time during that period, perhaps because of your impression that Mr. Nikolic was in charge of the military police, did you ever contact Colonel Blagojevic to make a particular request. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: No meaning you never contacted him?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to make sure that I'm clear. Did you contact him and say: I need you to issue an order for me to use the military police?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you for clarifying that. Now, after 1992, what other functions did you have with respect to your political positions in that community of Bratunac? You said that you were president of the Crisis Staff, and of course that didn't last forever. At some point the Crisis Staff was dissolved. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During a period of time in 1992, an order came to the effect that the work of the party was frozen and that we had the power from the government and Republika Srpska as former members of the SDS. I think they simply wanted to shelter us from military obligations, so they gave us this function, which, practically speaking, wasn't a proper function at all. I didn't have a proper function until the work of the party started again.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And when was that?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in the spring of 1993, I think. And I became actively involved in the summer of 1992. A number of things had taken place in the meantime of personal nature involving my family, and I distanced myself to a great extent from those events.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: From 1993 to 1995, however, you did resume your participation in SDS politics as the president of the SDS in Bratunac. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. However, the work was not in full swing. 90 per cent of the membership were mobilised, so we -- only a small number of us met again. But there is a written document to that extent, and the topics of the discussion are contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, as far as executive -- organs of executive authority in Bratunac, can you please list them. Usually you have, you know, the government, the legislature, and the judiciary. So who governed Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If we could get a time frame.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: We're in 1993. I don't understand what is Mr. McCloskey's problem. If he would follow and listen to the chronology, we're in 1993. We've gotten through that 1992 period; he's resumed. I'm going step by step.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is a bouncing ball and it bounces everywhere. And it's very unclear where he's been, and I will sit down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, let's focus on 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, after the Crisis Staff has been dissolved and now once the SDS party is reignited and rejuvenated and back in full swing, 1993, 1994, 1995, that period of time what I'm talking about is, what was the executive authority in Bratunac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But everything that other municipalities have, the president of the municipality, the president of the Executive Board, chiefs of very departments and affairs. I don't know about the court. I don't think it worked at the time. We had problems with human resources. Maybe it did work. I cannot remember anything. The police, of course, the Territorial Defence, the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And you did not hold a position within any of those organs?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Once again, I've said this for ten times I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But is it not a fact that the president of the municipality and the president of the Executive Board would come to you, to your office, to discuss matters of local politics?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is a fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And de facto speaking, okay, not de jure but de facto-wise, you had more power in Bratunac than they did during that period?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I should say yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Thank you. And you had a budget, I take it, that was provided by the party?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never had a proper account. That was a unique example in Bosnia-Herzegovina. We closed the account at one point, and we never reopened it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, were you getting paid a salary from the SDS?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a while I was getting some kind of compensation, which was paid from the budget of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Did you not have a car and a driver?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never had a driver. As for a car, I don't remember when it was that we bought it. It was late in time. A second-hand car was bought by the municipality and it was given to the SDS. I don't know when, 1993, maybe, 1994. 1994 I think it was. And again, I never had a driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was not Bratunac in essence, was not Bratunac in essence run by the SDS party with you being above the Executive Board and the mayor?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's only natural that during that period when Muslims and SDA left Bratunac and after the participation in the assembly stopped, we established the assembly with the remainder of the deputies. And of course the SDS was the dominant party. As its president, I had influence over the events the Bratunac, pursuant to the statutory provisions. I had influence over certain appointments, things having to do with the human resources, policy. Yes, I agree that that was my function.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Who gets to have a job with a salary working for the municipality. I mean you -- it would be fair to say that you were by far the most powerful figure in Bratunac, if not de jure, de facto for sure?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must give you a negative answer. Had I been so powerful, I would not have been arrested two times, taken to an execution, beaten up, intimidated and threatened. All kind of things happened to me. How can you then explain this power that you claim I had.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Was that happening around 1995, the events that you just described?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Some of these events, such as physical assaults, assassination attempt, took place in 1992. One of the arrests took place in 1993, another in 1994. A court-martial, that was in 1994, but no, not in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: In 1995, in and around the period of July, would it be fair to say that you were the most powerful individual, political-wise that is to say, in the Bratunac municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know how other people saw me. I cannot give you a comment on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, could the ordinary citizen just drive down to Pale and have a tete-a-tete with President Karadzic, as you did for instance - as you claim - on July 9 -- 8 or 9, 1995?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you're an educated man, and you are familiar with the fact that functions imply certain privileges as well. I was the president of the municipal chapter of SDS. Obviously I had the possibility to have an audience with the president and talk to him. I don't interpret this to be a special power. Whether an ordinary citizen could do that, I don't know. There may have been cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But you exercised those privileges, did you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't call them privileges, but the possibilities that I had as part of my function. And I did use them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, let's speak about on one of those occasions where you did use them. As I indicated, the date is unclear according to you whether it was on July 8th or July 9th, you paid a visit to President Karadzic in Pale. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I would include the 7th as well as a possibility. But we will compare to -- we will -- I will check the date with respect to testimonies in other cases as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But as I understand it, your frame of reference for the particular date is that on the following day after the meeting, you were able to accomplish one of your goals, which was to have Mr. Borovcanin come to the Bratunac area to assist in the attack of Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I referred to that, although I'm not sure. And I have information the effect that Borovcanin did not arrive on the 10th, but 11th in Bratunac. But I did refer to that because I knew that he arrived in Bratunac immediately after that. So it was on the basis of that that I concluded what the date could be. However, today I am almost certain that it was either on the 7th or the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. But at some point you said it was the day after Borovcanin arrived, so it could also be the 10th that you met with --

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before Borovcanin arrived, not after. The day after Borovcanin arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But if Borovcanin arrived on the 11th, having received an order dated the 10th, then it would be somewhere between the 9th and the 10th that you most likely visited, if you are correct in your -- if your memory is serving you correct that almost immediately Borovcanin arrived. Right?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You see, you say yourself that the order for Borovcanin was dated the 10th. So it had to be earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Be that as it may, according to your testimony in previous cases in your statements, you were in the field where you were able to observe Lieutenant Colonel Pandurevic and I believe the individual who was in charge of the Drina Wolves. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you as an untrained military officer, but nonetheless a president of the SDS, you had come to the conclusion that the situation wasn't going so well in the field and that they needed some more professional help, a more robust, shall we say, unit. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. But I was not alone and I did not make those assessments alone. I was assisted by Mr. Sinisa Glogovac who was with me at the time and he had more experience in that field than I had. And at the end of the day I had opportunity to see with my own eyes an attack of the hostile forces, the Muslim forces from Srebrenica, there were casualties on our side. The events were pretty complex, and I drew the conclusions I drew.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And this individual, by the way, he's not military; he's civilian as well, is he not, Mr. Glogovac?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was head of a section of the state security, which is a civilian service. I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So from one civilian to the next - and I'm not disputing whether he had more experience than you in interpreting battles -- nonetheless, you took it upon yourself to leave the line where you were observing and to drive, unannounced, unscheduled, unanticipated, to meet with President Karadzic in Pale. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Although, to this day I am not sure whether I had called him up before going there to announce my arrival. I think there's a good chance I went unannounced, as you say.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, as you said, not as I say. As you have said that you have gone there -- you went there unannounced because Pale is a small town and President Karadzic spent most of his time there during the war, and so chances were that that's where he would have been and that's why you had gone there unannounced. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. And I suspect that if someone can just show up and have a meeting with the president, he or she must be rather important or powerful or meaningful?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, can't you understand, Mr. Karnavas, that the events in Srebrenica themselves gave me importance. I do not dispute that I was president of the SDS with the accompanying authority and powers and that I knew Mr. Karadzic. But the military operation around Srebrenica was what gave me importance, weight, and the ability to see the president, as I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But the mayor didn't go or the president of the Executive Board didn't go, they didn't have that same power, that same access to power as you did. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We are now getting involved in a very odd discussion. The mayor had his own job, and it was relieved of the conundrum of day-to-day activities running a municipality. How can the president go to a front line? That's why I went to Pale. If he had gone to Pale instead of me, I am certain that he would have been equally received by the president.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Incidentally, you could have ordered him to go to Pale, but he could not have ordered you to go to Pale?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm saying it. I'm saying it. Based on your de facto powers, you could have ordered him or suggested him and he would have complied, but he could not order you to go there. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, you are establishing my de facto power. You are not giving me three days to go into details and see what my actual power was. And I understand why you won't allow me to explain, because it doesn't go in your favour. When we talk about power, we would have to see first how large my power was, how great it was. But since we cannot do that, then it's very difficult for me to have this discussion with you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You had a meeting -- you went to Pale unannounced, and at that point in time as I understand it, you were able to have a private conversation with the president. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, whichever way you wish to put it. The question is pretty pointless, if you'll excuse my saying so. You said you had the opportunity to have that conversation. I had it, which means I had the opportunity, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Karnavas --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm moving on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: We have already visited this area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Based on your testimony, you have indicated that when you went there to have this meeting with President Karadzic, you were totally in the dark as to what the mission was with respect to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I had my ideas, but I did not know what the precise objective regarding Srebrenica was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: So you as the main man in Bratunac at that period of time had not been given a clue from President Karadzic as to what the mission was going to be in the attack on Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We've been over this as well, Your Honour. And -- last time he referred to him as the number one man, I think, and we had a little argument over that. We've been over this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Karnavas, I believe --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll go on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- you could come directly to your point.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Prior to this, you claim, you claim, that you had a conversation with Karadzic sometime in May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And during that time you claim - we have no substantiation, we have no documents, we have nothing to verify - but you claim at that point in time --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection, argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: At that point in time -- I don't have any documents, Your Honour. I have nothing from the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: That would suggest that at that time, Mr. Deronjic, Mr. Karadzic forecasted that something was going to happen in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Such innuendo is just argumentative and appears to be designed to inflame the situation, which is not necessary and I would object to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I think your question is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: But the question is how to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'll rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: -- present it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: You indicated in the past that you had a meeting with Mr. Karadzic sometime in May. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And you have asserted that during that meeting President Karadzic told you that something would happen in Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Among other things, yes. One part of our conversation regarded the status of General Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Right. Because - and I'm glad you mentioned Zivanovic - because you as the president of the SDS of Bratunac were not getting along with the commander of the Drina Corps at the time, General Zivanovic. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With what he was doing, rather. I had no problem with him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But nonetheless, you kept complaining to Karadzic, and this had been an issue where you were asking President Karadzic to remove General Zivanovic from his post. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because that disagreement had gone a long way. I insisted and asked President Karadzic to remove him a long time before that. And if you say that I was so powerful, how do you explain that he, Karadzic, hadn't done it much earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Deronjic, at that time you claim that that is when you were told that something would happen in Srebrenica, but you weren't told exactly what would happen. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But you were told, nonetheless, to make provisions for something that you weren't aware of what was going to happen?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew there would be a military operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. So now you're claiming for the first time that President Karadzic told you, We will have a military operation on Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what terms I used before, but all the time - and we can look in the transcripts - military operation was implied. We certainly weren't talking about a cultural event. What other operation could be meant?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, all right. I assume when he told you that some kind of military operation, whether it was implied or direct, I assume you, being responsible for those folks back in Bratunac and given your position, you might have asked, What kind? What exactly do you have in mind, Mr. President, because I need to make some provisions? What are we planning? Did you ask that question directly to the president of the RS at the time, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Around Srebrenica in the period we're talking about from 1992 to 1995, there were countless operations involving development of obstacles, attacks, and so on and so forth. We were not sitting in a meeting talking on that particular occasion. We were leaving a building and we were talking about Zivanovic for the most part, and that's when he said there would be a military operation around Srebrenica. And if there's anything you think you should do in terms of preparations, go on and do it. I didn't that I was to mount God knows what in terms of preparations. I understood it to mean help the army and do whatever you think fit, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So nonetheless, on the 9th or the 8th or the 7th or whatever the date is that you went to Pale -- that is to July, not knowing exactly what the goal was, you had nonetheless come to the conclusion that whatever the operation was, it simply wasn't going well and you needed somebody from Bratunac, an acquaintance of yours, Mr. Borovcanin to come and to assist on the attack in Srebrenica. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But let me just explain one thing. When I was on that forward command post observing with my own eyes, I noticed a couple of very strange things. Commander Pandurevic was there, nicknamed Legend; General Krstic, who I saw for the first time there, and I didn't know there was a replacement, either de jure or de facto. I noticed a number of things that I didn't like, so I thought I should go to the president. And I thought that in view of the intensity of the operation which resulted in a number of deaths already, maybe we should involve a serious unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. Well, another way of interpreting your visit could be also - and this is what I'm putting to you - that you chose a personal friend or a personal acquaintance who happened to be from the civilian sector, not the military, and you were making the suggestion as Srebrenica was falling so that the civilian sector could claim part of the victory in the fall of Srebrenica, as opposed to letting the military under General Zivanovic take all the credit. Is that not another interpretation, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, it was during this occasion, as I understand it, this meeting that you had, that there was another conversation that took place with respect to what, if anything, you should do, whether it was you in the plural meaning out of respect or you the members of the executive authority in Bratunac, what you should do with the civilian population if the -- if Srebrenica were to fall. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: It would be fair to say, would it not, that we have no other verification of the contents of that conversation, other than you?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is another source, and that's Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: But he's not here?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: All right. So other than Mr. Karadzic, we would have to accept you for telling the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth with respect to this unsubstantiated alleged conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Objection. That's a misstatement of the facts. The civilians were butchered as everyone knows. So I would say it was fairly substantiated to that degree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, I know it's late today, but I don't think those adjectives are necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Can you provide us with some substantiation that this conversation took place? And I'm not referring to the documents that the Prosecutor gave that you reviewed with your lawyers in order to come up with some theory into how you can get a good sentence for yourself. I'm saying, did you have a tape recorder, do you have a note in your diary, do you have something that would tell us that this conversation took place and that this is what President Karadzic told you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well -- yes, Mr. McCloskey? Okay, Witness, you may answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: He wants to answer the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, let's hear Mr. McCloskey is going to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No witness should ever have to put up, no matter what they have done, with that kind of question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: What's the problem with the question? I'm asking if he has a tape-recording, he's got a diary, if there's a document, something that would say we had this conversation and this is what the president said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a fine question, but the part about his lawyers cooking up deals is so over the top.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We are not satisfied with that phrase in order to come up with some theories into so on and so forth. It is unnecessary to add this sentence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honours --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Maybe you want to put some pressures on this witness, but it's really not necessary to mention that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't have the document in front of me where the gentleman does indicate that after going through these documents he's able to now fill in the blanks. I'm not suggesting that his lawyers did anything, but his lawyers provided him with the documents without him getting indicted. He didn't have the disclosure material. The disclosure material as a result of having lawyers was provided to him. He fills in the blanks, not the lawyers. There's no suggestion that the lawyers are doing anything wrong. But as I started by cross-examination, I hit that point very hard as far as him wanting to know, what exactly did I say that caused you to make me now a suspect. Can you give me that information? His own lawyer at that very meeting said, give us the documents so we can study them so he can be prepared. He has to get indicted, he has to get the disclosure material. And there all of a sudden we see a shift of the story, a memory that somehow becomes much more credible than the one before where he's had months and months and years and years to prepare. And by his own admission, Your Honour, he sat around with his friends --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to interrupt at this point. It's absolutely inappropriate for him to demean the witness in his presence. If he wishes to make any demeaning arguments to any witness in the Court, I would ask that the witness be left out of the room.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm putting that to the witness, Your Honour. That is the conclusion of my cross-examination. This is what I will put to the witness. And Mr. McCloskey has cautioned me once that I'm not putting questions to the witness, so that's what I'm doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I believe it's pretty late at this stage, so will you please rephrase your question and let us finish the sitting for this morning. I understand that there's another trial waiting for the use of this courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Other than you, sir, telling us here that this conversation took place and the contents of the conversation, particularly as to the Western Slavonia principle, do you have anything concretely that would give us some assurances that that conversation did in fact take place, and that if it did take place that President Karadzic told you specifically, exactly what you have claimed he has said?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I was in a position maybe to add some arguments in favour of that theory. I don't have my lawyer here. I don't want to create an unpleasantry here. But there were a couple of people in the vicinity then whom I ran into again in prison. He asked me why I mentioned that date, and I said, Do you mind? Do you think it's untrue? He said, No. He said according to his notes and documents, it should be the 7th. And this conversation was overheard by another prisoner. I want to discuss this matter further with my lawyers, and then we could perhaps revisit these facts when I testify again. I have no other documents. I don't even understand what you are talking about. What kind of recording could I possibly have, video recording at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Well, thank you for answering the question at the end, that is there is no other documentation, other than your word?

utterances.speaker: MIROSLAV DERONJIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For the time being, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Given that answer, Your Honour, I would ask that a caution be issued to the witness that he is not to have any conversations with his lawyers with respect to this. In fact, I would ask over an abundance of caution that he not have any contact with his lawyers at all, because I don't want there to be any problems. Now, if he wishes -- another alternative may be for a representative of the Registrar to be there to make sure that they are not talking about the substance of his testimony. Because as I understand it, that's forbidden. That's the Rule.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Karnavas, I don't think your request is reasonable or not entirely reasonable. I believe that Mr. Deronjic is entitled to consult with his counsel, especially on the legal issues, but not on the factual issues.
